d: In Dignano: a cross of alleys within modestly apparent houses, some with very pretty Venetian windows in the sharp arches, others with very light cornices and slender shelves with supports, - these have internal porch, those stone staircases outside. In the acute arches of the doors and porticoes images of the Madonna with lamps and flowers or framed by bizarre braids of ears and fronds. To the right the house of Menico, which occupies the first floor of the scene and is casuccia distinctly dignanese with small porch steps and with the porch pe 'which you can see the inside of the courtyard; - behind this other houses and streets. To the left the house of Bara Giacomo, and a tavern with rough benches at the sides of its door; - and other houses opening to other streets. In the bottom a leak of houses behind which the gray bell bells the girgs of the black sky, the roofed church is by Gignano.

Biagio comes from a street on the left talking animatedly with Nicola, a handsome young man, and, although dressed in dignanese fashion, though not without a certain refinement; Biagio instead is an odd old man, looking at and talking bizarre and of a comedy coming from nature and the rest from the necessity of existence. Nicola leaves Biagio and sits ahead of the tavern with other young people. - Biagio goes under the windows of the house of Menico.
Menico comes out, a man of always corraced face on which must never have passed the serene of a good laugh even in the days of youth.

People, males with males and females come to groups with females; Men, Children and Old, Women, Girls and Girls; they come from the left street and come back from the church. Men have the headband on their shoulders (jacket without sacks), wide flat wing hats and yellow leather shoes.

In the People who pass by and cross the bottom of the scene, appears a Slavic Maiden. - It is certain Luze of the surroundings of Peroi, a small village near Dignano, inhabited by a colony of Montenegrin who fled from the mountains there they took refuge between the sea and Prostimus (a sad and uncultivable place, where they do not vegetate that wild strawberries, juniper, thyme and heathers) and, always forming among the people of their husbands, they have been up to our days spread pure and in the blood and rite of their religion. Pass among the People the Young and offers bouquets of wild strawberries: it offers them to all and also to Biagio who returns from where he accompanied Nicola to the house of coffin Giacomo.
In the meantime it is evening - some peasants still pass - some women go down and light the lamps to the Madonnas and come back closing the exits.
Marussa descends into the courtyard through the inner door, where, coming from the side street to the house of Menico, Lorenzo is introduced almost immediately.

The procession that leads the bride Menina to the home of her husband, the Son of Coffin Giacomo, comes from the bottom. The procession is preceded by an old man with a light in his hands. Some carry torches. There is Biagio who squeezes his violin. The bride is all moved by the abandonment of the house, but she wants to hide her emotion, but, as is the custom of the Dignano, the Invited around make her gazzarre crying to make her cry.
While the two Lovers hold their hand to break up, here is Menico!

In the house of Menico. Spacious room on the first floor where he usually keeps the family dignanese. In the bottom two doors. The one on the left, having on the upper door a small altar with a painted plaster Madonna, puts to the room of Marussa; the other on the right puts to the staircase for which you go down to the lower rooms. Between the two doors a large hood adorned with a curtain of white mussola; on the frame there are several terracotta crockery. On the chain that hangs from the fireplace is a boiler. In the middle of the room a table, and rustic chairs; on the left wall a straw canapè; on the right two windows looking on the street. Between the two windows a wooden bench with two copper buckets. The wall above the bench is decorated with plates and copper tools. On the left wall two paintings. From the ceiling hang in large number of panicles tied to bunches. Marussa comes in with a basket of wire on her head, but as soon as she lays it, she notices her father.
Marussa comes out with the Colleghe.

Marussa's chamber. Marussa has already worn the skirt and the body of the wedding garment; all the rest of her wedding dress, the veil, the flowers etc., is placed on her bed. Marussa's bedroom has two entrances, one at the bottom and is supposed to put to the room in which the second act took place, so that, from the open door, the public can see it; the other side. A window gives you light. The modest bed has white muslin curtains, its blanket is white as well; everything is of a surprising whiteness and sharpness. A few chairs - a table - a singer and a mirror leaning over the window. At the rising of the canvas Marussa is sitting in front of the mirror and adapting the conciere.
Nicola enters with great enthusiasm, but still saw Marussa undressed and scarred stops surprised.
